pos: a. (upright, seemly, of good repute; in the Authorized Version chiefly what is comely and creditable before men as well as before God)
etymology: From Latin honestus, honourable, from honos, honour, through Old French honeste. In 1611 English the word still carried its Latin breadth — not merely “not a thief” but honourable, seemly, of good report. The Greek behind it is kalos, beautiful or noble, and semnos, grave and venerable.
biblical_def: The Authorized Version uses honest where modern speech would say honourable. Our Lord names the soil that bears fruit as “an honest and good heart” (Luke 8:15) — not a heart that has ceased to lie, but a heart made noble, sound, and fit to hold the word. The apostle commands a public quality of life: “Provide things honest in the sight of all men” (Romans 12:17), and again, “Providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men” (2 Corinthians 8:21). The setting of that second verse is the handling of the Macedonian collection; Paul would not carry other men's money alone, and the deliberate transparency he built into the arrangement is what he calls honest. The word therefore reaches past private integrity into visible, checkable conduct. It enters Paul's catalogue of what the sanctified mind is to dwell upon: “whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just” (Philippians 4:8). Peter presses the same thing on strangers in a hostile world — “Having your conversation honest among the Gentiles” (1 Peter 2:12) — so that slander would be refuted by the plain look of the thing. Honesty in Scripture is never merely negative. It is the fruit of a regenerate heart, made visible.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives honest first as upright and just in dealing, then as decent, honourable, and suitable — the broad sense the Authorized Version carries.
webster_full: HONEST, a. on'est. Upright; just; fair in dealing with others; free from trickishness and fraud; acting and having acted the part of a just man.
2. Fair; just; equitable; free from fraud.
3. Decent; honorable; suitable to the character or station.
4. Frank; sincere; unreserved; as an honest countenance.
HONESTY, n. In principle, an upright disposition; moral rectitude of heart; a disposition to conform to justice and correct moral principles, in all social transactions.
scriptures: Luke 8:15
But that on the good ground are they, which in an honest and good heart, having heard the word, keep it, and bring forth fruit with patience.
Romans 12:17
Recompense to no man evil for evil. Provide things honest in the sight of all men.
2 Corinthians 8:21
Providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men.
1 Peter 2:12
Having your conversation honest among the Gentiles: that, whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God in the day of visitation.
corruption_summary: Honesty has been shrunk to blunt self-disclosure — “I'm just being honest” — which licenses cruelty and excuses nothing.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern use of the word has collapsed into a single narrow act: saying out loud whatever one presently feels. On that reckoning a man is honest when he tells his wife exactly what he thinks of her, and the phrase I'm just being honest becomes a licence rather than a claim. Scripture will not have it. The honest man of Romans 12:17 is the man who provides things honest in the sight of all men — whose accounts, promises, workmanship, and reputation will bear inspection. Blunt speech that wounds without love is not honesty; it is what Proverbs calls the piercing of a sword, and the tongue of the wise is set against it.

The opposite error is equally common in the church: an honesty confined to the heart, invisible to the neighbour, resting on the claim that God alone sees. Paul refuses that too. He arranged the Jerusalem collection so that men as well as the Lord could see the handling of it, because a ministry above suspicion is part of the ministry itself. Where elders, deacons, and treasurers decline that visibility, appealing to their own sincerity, the word honest in its Authorized sense has already been lost. Recover it and much else follows: open books, kept promises, work done when no one is watching, and a reputation that will not have to be defended.
roots_summary: Greek kalos, good or noble — Luke 8:15, Romans 12:17, 1 Peter 2:12; semnos, grave and honourable — Philippians 4:8; agathos, good — Luke 8:15.
roots_lines: Greek kalos — beautiful, noble, of good report; the word rendered honest in Romans 12:17, 2 Corinthians 8:21 and 1 Peter 2:12.
Greek semnos — grave, venerable, worthy of reverence; Philippians 4:8, and the required character of deacons and aged men.
Greek agathos — good in substance; paired with kalos in Luke 8:15, “an honest and good heart.”
Hebrew yashar — straight, upright; the Old Testament root behind the same moral idea, as in Proverbs 11:3.
Latin honestus, from honos, honour — the source of the English word and of its older, broader sense.
usage: “An honest and good heart” — the soil that keeps the word and bears fruit with patience.
“Provide things honest in the sight of all men” — visible, checkable conduct, not private sincerity.
Paul's handling of the collection: transparency built in beforehand, so that no man could suspect.

pos: a. (costly, precious, held at high value; used of Christ the Son, of the saints, and of a life a man may or may not count precious to himself)
etymology: Old English deore, precious or costly — the same root as dearth, since what is scarce is dear. The Greek is agapetos, beloved, the verbal adjective of agapao; the Hebrew is yaqqir, precious or costly.
biblical_def: Dear in the Authorized Version keeps its old commercial edge: a thing is dear when it costs much. So the Father's love for the Son is set out in the language of price — “Who hath delivered us from the power of darkness, and hath translated us into the kingdom of his dear Son” (Colossians 1:13). The kingdom into which the elect are translated is the kingdom of the Son whom the Father holds most precious, and that is the measure of the mercy. The same word describes the standing of the redeemed: “Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children” (Ephesians 5:1). Adoption is not bare legal transfer; the adopted are held dear, and the imitation commanded flows from that settled affection rather than from an attempt to earn it. The LORD uses the word of an apostate people He will not finally cast off: “Is Ephraim my dear son? is he a pleasant child?” (Jeremiah 31:20). And Paul turns the word against himself, weighing his own life on the same scale and finding it light: “neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy” (Acts 20:24). What is dear to God orders what may be counted dear by us.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dear first as of a high price, then as beloved and precious — both senses live in the Authorized Version.
webster_full: DEAR, a. Scarce; not plentiful; as a dear year.
2. Bearing a high price in comparison of the usual price; more costly than usual.
3. Of a high value in estimation; greatly beloved; precious.
4. Beloved; as a dear friend.
DEARTH, n. Scarcity; such a want of any thing as renders it dear.
scriptures: Colossians 1:13
Who hath delivered us from the power of darkness, and hath translated us into the kingdom of his dear Son:
Ephesians 5:1
Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children;
Jeremiah 31:20

Is Ephraim my dear son? is he a pleasant child? for since I spake against him, I do earnestly remember him still: therefore my bowels are troubled for him; I will surely have mercy upon him, saith the LORD.
Acts 20:24

But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God.
corruption_summary: Dear has decayed into a formality at the head of a letter, and the costly weight the word carried in 1611 is gone.
corruption_paragraphs: Nothing so drains a word as making it compulsory. Dear Sir at the head of a bill means nothing whatever, and the word has been worn smooth by the salutation until English readers pass over Colossians 1:13 without hearing it. The Authorized translators chose dear because it said costly. The kingdom of His dear Son is the kingdom of the Son whom the Father prizes above all, and the deliverance of sinners into that kingdom is measured by exactly that price. Where the word is heard as a politeness, the doctrine is heard as a pleasantry.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the loss is one of ordinary erosion rather than deliberate assault. The principle to recover is the old economy of the word. Nothing is dear that costs nothing. Adoption is dear because the Son was given; the church is dear because it was purchased with His own blood; and a man's own life, weighed against a course to be finished, is not dear at all. Paul's arithmetic in Acts 20:24 is only shocking to those who have forgotten what the word means.
roots_summary: Greek agapetos, beloved — Colossians 1:13, Ephesians 5:1; timios, precious or costly — Acts 20:24; Hebrew yaqqir, precious — Jeremiah 31:20.
roots_lines: Greek agapetos — beloved, the verbal adjective of agapao; rendered dear at Colossians 1:13 and Ephesians 5:1.
Greek timios — held at a price, precious; Acts 20:24, where Paul declines to price his own life highly.
Hebrew yaqqir — costly, precious, rare; Jeremiah 31:20 of Ephraim, and of precious stones elsewhere.
Old English deore — costly; the same root as dearth, scarcity being what makes a thing dear.
The commercial sense governs the theological one: what God holds dear He has paid for.
usage: “The kingdom of his dear Son” — the price of the kingdom stated in one adjective.
“As dear children” — the ground of imitation is settled affection, not probation.
“Neither count I my life dear unto myself” — Paul's valuation of his own life over against his course.

pos: a. (full of thanks; the settled disposition of a heart that acknowledges God as the giver of every good)
etymology: From Old English thanc, thought or grateful thought, with the suffix -ful. The Greek is eucharistos, from eu, well, and charis, grace — literally well-graced, one who returns grace for grace.
biblical_def: Thankfulness is commanded, not merely commended. “Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise: be thankful unto him, and bless his name” (Psalm 100:4) makes it the appointed manner of approach; the worshipper does not come to negotiate but to acknowledge. Paul makes it the rule of the peace-ruled heart: “And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to the which also ye are called in one body; and be ye thankful” (Colossians 3:15). The Greek word is eucharistos — well-graced — and it exposes the whole doctrine, for a man returns thanks only when he has understood that what he holds was given. Most decisive of all is the diagnosis in Romans 1: “when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened” (Romans 1:21). Ingratitude is not a small failure of manners at the edge of the fall; it stands in the indictment beside the refusal to glorify Him, and the darkening of the mind follows it. The thankful heart is therefore a mark of regeneration, and the settled thanklessness of the natural man is a symptom of what he is.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines thankful as grateful, and notes the word is chiefly applied to the acknowledgment of divine favour.
webster_full: THANKFUL, a. Grateful; impressed with a sense of kindness received, and ready to acknowledge it.
The Lord's people should be thankful for his mercies.
THANKFULNESS, n. Expression of gratitude; acknowledgment of a favor.
THANKSGIVING, n. The act of rendering thanks or expressing gratitude for favors or mercies.
2. A public celebration of divine goodness.
scriptures: Psalm 100:4
Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise: be thankful unto him, and bless his name.
Colossians 3:15
And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to the which also ye are called in one body; and be ye thankful.
Romans 1:21
Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened.
Colossians 2:7
Rooted and built up in him, and stablished in the faith, as ye have been taught, abounding therein with thanksgiving.
corruption_summary: Gratitude has been detached from any giver and marketed as a technique for well-being — thanks addressed to no one.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern gratitude industry keeps the posture and removes the Person. One is told to be grateful to the universe, or simply to practise gratitude as a discipline that improves sleep and lowers stress, and the exercise is defended entirely by its measured effects on the one performing it. Scripture knows nothing of thanks with no object. Be thankful unto him — the preposition is the doctrine. Gratitude to no one is a contradiction dressed as a virtue, and it is precisely the vanity Romans 1:21 describes: men who know God, decline to thank Him, and are handed over to their own imaginations.

The second corruption is subtler and lives inside the church. Thankfulness gets treated as an emotional weather report — something felt when circumstances are favourable and honestly unavailable when they are not. Paul commands it in prison. The peace of God ruling in the heart and the command be ye thankful stand in the same verse, and neither waits on circumstance. Recover the doctrine of providence and thankfulness follows; a man who believes that his Father governs every particular has ground for thanks in a hard year as well as an easy one.
roots_summary: Greek eucharistos, thankful — Colossians 3:15; eucharisteo, to give thanks — Romans 1:21; Hebrew todah, thanksgiving — Psalm 100:4.
roots_lines: Greek eucharistos — well-graced, thankful; Colossians 3:15, the only occurrence of the adjective in the New Testament.
Greek eucharisteo — to give thanks, from eu and charis; Romans 1:21, where the negative is the indictment.
Hebrew todah — thanksgiving, and the thank offering itself; Psalm 100:4 and Leviticus 7:12.
Hebrew yadah — to confess, to give thanks with extended hands; the root of todah.
Old English thanc — thought; gratitude is the mind remembering the giver.
usage: “Be thankful unto him” — the preposition carries the whole doctrine.
“Neither were thankful” — ingratitude listed among the first sins of the darkened mind.
Eucharistos: well-graced — thanks is grace returned for grace received.

pos: adv. (in a lowly manner; the required posture of a man before God, and the manner of walking Micah names)
etymology: From Latin humilis, low, from humus, the ground — the same earth from which Adam was taken. The Hebrew adverb at Micah 6:8 is tsana, to be modest or lowly, a rare verb occurring only twice in the Old Testament.
biblical_def: The word stands at the summit of the prophets' summary of true religion: “He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?” (Micah 6:8). Three things are required, and the third governs the other two, for justice without lowliness hardens into self-righteousness and mercy without lowliness becomes condescension. The Hebrew verb behind humbly is rare — it carries the sense of walking circumspectly, modestly, as one who knows whose company he keeps. The New Testament states the same requirement as a command with a promise attached twice over: “Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up” (James 4:10), and “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time” (1 Peter 5:6). Both make the humbling active and the exalting God's. The Reformed reading of Micah 6:8 has always refused the modern use of it as a summary of religion apart from atonement; the verse comes in the middle of a covenant lawsuit in which the LORD prosecutes His people, and the humility required is the humility of the guilty before the offended Judge who alone provides the ransom.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines humbly as in a humble manner, with modest submission, without pride or arrogance.
webster_full: HUMBLY, adv. In a humble manner; with modest submissiveness; with humility.
2. With modest respect; without arrogance.
HUMBLE, a. Low; opposed to high or lofty.
2. Low; opposed to lofty or great; mean; not magnificent; as a humble cottage.
3. Modest; meek; submissive; opposed to proud, haughty, arrogant or assuming.
scriptures: Micah 6:8
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
James 4:10
Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up.
1 Peter 5:6
Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time:
2 Samuel 16:4
Then said the king to Ziba, Behold, thine are all that pertained unto Mephibosheth. And Ziba said, I humbly beseech thee that I may find grace in thy sight, my lord, O king.
corruption_summary: Micah 6:8 is quoted as a gospel-free ethic, and humility itself is redefined as low self-assessment rather than submission to God.
corruption_paragraphs: Micah 6:8 is the most frequently detached verse in the English Bible. Printed on banners and lifted out of its covenant lawsuit, it becomes a programme of social ethics that requires no atonement, no repentance, and no God who judges — three duties any decent man might discharge without a Saviour. Read in place, the verse is the LORD's answer to a people asking what sacrifice could possibly cover their guilt: thousands of rams, ten thousands of rivers of oil, the firstborn for their transgression. The answer is not be nicer; it is that God has already shewn what is good and their offerings were never the difficulty. To walk humbly with God is to come to Him on His terms — which the whole prophetic corpus, and Hebrews after it, says means the blood He appointed and not the blood men chose.

The second corruption redefines humility as a low opinion of oneself, a psychological state to be cultivated by self-deprecation. That is not what the word means. Humilis is low to the ground; the posture is relational, not introspective. A man may hold a very poor opinion of himself and still be unbending toward God, and men often do; the word for that is despair, not humility. James and Peter both make the movement active and directional — humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, under the mighty hand of God — and both attach the lifting up to Him, not to the exercise.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsana, to be lowly — Micah 6:8; Greek tapeinoo, to make low — James 4:10, 1 Peter 5:6; Latin humilis, from humus, ground.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsana — to be modest, to walk circumspectly; Micah 6:8, one of only two Old Testament occurrences.
Greek tapeinoo — to bring low, to humble; James 4:10 and 1 Peter 5:6, both in the imperative.
Greek tapeinophrosune — lowliness of mind; Philippians 2:3, the mind that was in Christ Jesus.
Latin humilis, from humus, the ground — the same dust of which Adam was formed.
Micah 6:8 sits inside a covenant lawsuit; the humility required is the humility of the guilty before the Judge.
usage: “To walk humbly with thy God” — the third requirement, which governs the first two.
“Humble yourselves… and he shall lift you up” — the humbling is ours, the exalting His.
Humilis, from humus: low to the ground, not low in self-esteem.

pos: adv. (in accordance with justice; of conduct that renders to each what is due, and of a sentence rightly deserved)
etymology: From Latin justus, righteous or lawful, from jus, right or law. The Hebrew at Micah 6:8 is mishpat, judgment; the Greek at 1 Thessalonians 2:10 is dikaios, and at Luke 23:41 the same root, righteously.
biblical_def: To do justly is the first of the three requirements of Micah 6:8 — “to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God.” The Hebrew word is mishpat, the judgment or verdict, and to do it is to give every man his due in weight, wage, judgment, and word. Paul appeals to the same standard as a witness to his own ministry: “Ye are witnesses, and God also, how holily and justly and unblameably we behaved ourselves among you that believe” (1 Thessalonians 2:10), where three adverbs cover the whole field — toward God, toward men, and before any accuser. The most piercing use of the word is on the cross. The penitent thief rebukes his fellow with it: “And we indeed justly; for we receive the due reward of our deeds: but this man hath done nothing amiss” (Luke 23:41). In one sentence he confesses the justice of his own condemnation and the innocence of the Man beside him, and that double confession is the substance of saving faith. Justice, biblically, is not first a programme for society but an attribute of God — “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?” (Genesis 18:25) — and human justice is derivative, measured by His law, never by shifting consensus.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines justly as in a just manner, according to right and law, and also as accurately or by right measure.
webster_full: JUSTLY, adv. In conformity to law, justice or propriety; by right.
2. In an exact manner; accurately; precisely.
3. Honestly; fairly.
JUST, a. Regular; orderly; due; suitable.
2. Exactly proportioned; as just weights and a just measure.
scriptures: Micah 6:8
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
Luke 23:41
And we indeed justly; for we receive the due reward of our deeds: but this man hath done nothing amiss.
1 Thessalonians 2:10
Ye are witnesses, and God also, how holily and justly and unblameably we behaved ourselves among you that believe:
Genesis 18:25

That be far from thee to do after this manner, to slay the righteous with the wicked: and that the righteous should be as the wicked, that be far from thee: Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?
corruption_summary: Justice has been severed from God's unchanging law and reassigned to group grievance, so that the word now names an outcome rather than a standard.
corruption_paragraphs: The dominant modern usage treats justice as a distribution to be achieved among groups rather than a standard by which persons are judged. On that account a verdict is just when the resulting arrangement pleases, and unjust when it does not — which is to say the standard has been replaced by the outcome. Scripture will not permit it. Mishpat is a verdict rendered according to a fixed law, and the law expressly forbids partiality in both directions: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty. A justice that must first ask who the parties are before it can render a judgment is the very thing Leviticus prohibits. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: names the framework in order to rebut it

Against every shifting definition stands Abraham's question: Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right? It assumes that God has a character, that His character is the standard, and that Abraham may reason from it. This is why the cross is the great vindication of justice and not its suspension. God did not overlook sin to be merciful; He punished it in the Substitute, that He might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus. The thief on the cross understood in an hour what a great deal of modern theology has lost: we indeed justly, and this man hath done nothing amiss.
roots_summary: Hebrew mishpat, judgment — Micah 6:8; Greek dikaios, righteous, and its adverb — Luke 23:41, 1 Thessalonians 2:10; Latin justus, from jus, law.
roots_lines: Hebrew mishpat — judgment, verdict, the due sentence; Micah 6:8, “to do justly.”
Hebrew tsedeq — righteousness, the standard by which the verdict is measured; Deuteronomy 16:20.
Greek dikaios — just, righteous; its adverbial form at 1 Thessalonians 2:10 and Luke 23:41.
Greek dikaioo — to justify, to declare righteous; the courtroom verb behind Romans 3:26.
Latin justus, from jus, right or law — justice measured by a law outside the parties.
usage: “To do justly” — rendering each his due in weight, wage, and judgment.
“We indeed justly” — the thief confesses his sentence deserved and Christ innocent.
“Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?” — justice grounded in God's character.

pos: adv. (with mildness and care; of the Shepherd leading those with young, and of a king's order concerning a rebel son)
etymology: From Latin gentilis, of the same clan, through Old French gentil, well-born — the manner supposed proper to good birth. The Hebrew at Isaiah 40:11 is nahal, to lead to a watering place, to guide with care.
biblical_def: Two occurrences carry the word in the Authorized Version, and they are worth setting side by side. The first is a command from a father who is also a king, given about a son in armed rebellion against him: “Deal gently for my sake with the young man, even with Absalom” (2 Samuel 18:5). It is an order the army heard and disobeyed, and the grief that follows is among the heaviest in Scripture. The second is prophecy of the LORD Himself: “He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young” (Isaiah 40:11). The Hebrew nahal means to lead at the pace the weakest can bear — the ewe heavy with young sets the speed of the flock, not the strong. This comes immediately after the announcement that the LORD God will come with a strong hand and His arm shall rule for Him; the same arm that rules gathers lambs. Gentleness in Scripture is therefore never weakness, but strength governed. The New Testament requires it of ministers — “the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men” (2 Timothy 2:24) — and of any man restoring another taken in a fault.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines gently as softly, meekly, mildly, without harshness or violence.
webster_full: GENTLY, adv. Softly; meekly; mildly; with tenderness.
2. Without violence, roughness or asperity.
GENTLE, a. Well born; of a good family or respectable birth, though not noble.
2. Mild; meek; soft; bland; not rough, harsh or severe.
3. Tame; peaceable; not wild, turbulent or refractory.
scriptures: Isaiah 40:11
He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young.
2 Samuel 18:5

And the king commanded Joab and Abishai and Ittai, saying, Deal gently for my sake with the young man, even with Absalom. And all the people heard when the king gave all the captains charge concerning Absalom.
2 Timothy 2:24
And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient,
Galatians 6:1
Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.
corruption_summary: Gentleness is mistaken for mildness of doctrine, so that a man is called gentle when he has merely declined to say anything true.
corruption_paragraphs: A widespread confusion identifies gentleness with agreeableness — a manner that avoids conflict by avoiding content. On that account the gentle pastor is the one who never names a sin, and firmness of doctrine is heard as harshness by definition. The text will not support it. 2 Timothy 2:24 puts gentle unto all men in the same breath as apt to teach, and the sentence continues into instructing those that oppose themselves. Isaiah's Shepherd is the same LORD whose arm rules for Him. Gentleness is strength that has taken the measure of the weak and adjusted its pace; a man with no strength to govern is not gentle, only ineffectual.

The opposite error deserves equal attention, since Reformed men are more prone to it. Sound doctrine held without nahal — without leading the flock at the pace the heavy-laden can bear — scatters the very sheep it means to feed. Galatians 6:1 gives the rule for the hardest case: a brother overtaken in a fault is to be restored, and restored in the spirit of meekness, with the restorer watching himself. Joab thought the kingdom was better served by killing Absalom, and he may even have been right about the politics; he was disobeying his king, and the king wept.
roots_summary: Hebrew nahal, to lead to water, to guide gently — Isaiah 40:11; lat, softly — 2 Samuel 18:5; Greek epios, mild — 2 Timothy 2:24.
roots_lines: Hebrew nahal — to lead to a resting or watering place, at the pace the weak can keep; Isaiah 40:11.
Hebrew lat — softly, secretly, gently; 2 Samuel 18:5, the king's charge concerning Absalom.
Greek epios — mild, gentle as a nurse with children; 2 Timothy 2:24 and 1 Thessalonians 2:7.
Greek prautes — meekness, strength under control; Galatians 6:1, the spirit in which a brother is restored.
Latin gentilis, of the clan — the manner thought proper to good birth, whence English gentle.
usage: “Shall gently lead those that are with young” — the flock moves at the ewe's pace, not the ram's.
“Deal gently… with the young man” — a father's order for a son in rebellion, and disobeyed.
“Gentle unto all men, apt to teach” — gentleness and doctrine in the same sentence.

pos: a. (without blemish or defect; used of the covenant that was not, and of the saints who shall be presented so)
etymology: From fault — Latin fallere, to deceive or fail, through Old French faute, a lack — with the suffix -less. The Greek is amemptos, unblamed, and amomos, without spot, the sacrificial word for an unblemished victim.
biblical_def: The Authorized Version uses faultless twice, and each time the word is doing heavy doctrinal work. The first is a negative verdict on the old covenant: “For if that first covenant had been faultless, then should no place have been sought for the second” (Hebrews 8:7). The fault, as the next verse makes plain, was found with them and not with the law — the covenant of works could not produce what it required, because the material it worked upon was fallen. The second is the doxology of Jude: “Now unto him that is able to keep you from falling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy” (Jude 24). Here the Greek is amomos, the very word used of a lamb without blemish fit for the altar, and the astonishing claim is that sinners will be so presented. Note who does it. The saint does not make himself faultless and offer himself; God is able to keep and God presents. This is perseverance and glorification stated in one sentence, and it is the answer to Hebrews 8:7 — what the first covenant could not accomplish, the second does, because its Mediator is the spotless Lamb whose righteousness is imputed to those He keeps.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines faultless as without fault, free from defect or blemish, perfect.
webster_full: FAULTLESS, a. Without fault; not defective or imperfect; free from blemish; free from incorrectness; perfect.
Whoever thinks a faultless piece to see, thinks what ne'er was, nor is, nor e'er shall be.
FAULT, n. Properly, a failing or falling; whence, defect; imperfection.
2. A slight offense; a neglect of duty or propriety.
BLEMISH, n. Any mark of deformity; any scar or defect that diminishes beauty.
scriptures: Hebrews 8:7
For if that first covenant had been faultless, then should no place have been sought for the second.
Jude 1:24
Now unto him that is able to keep you from falling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy,
Philippians 2:15
That ye may be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights in the world;
Ephesians 5:27
That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish.
corruption_summary: Perfectionism claims the faultlessness of Jude 24 for the present life, and the opposite error treats it as a figure of speech that never becomes fact.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors flank this word. The first is perfectionism — the Wesleyan and later holiness claim that entire sanctification may be attained in this life, so that a believer becomes actually faultless before death. Jude 24 will not fund it: the presenting is future, it is done before the presence of his glory, and it is God who does it. The whole New Testament testimony to the ongoing warfare of Romans 7 and Galatians 5 stands against a present sinlessness, and the pastoral damage done by teaching it has been enormous, driving honest men to despair and dishonest men to pretence.

The second error is to let the promise evaporate. Faultlessness is treated as a legal fiction or a devotional flourish, never an actual state. But Scripture means it. The church will be presented without spot or wrinkle; the saints will be presented faultless with exceeding joy; the imputed righteousness of Christ received now by faith will be matched by an imparted holiness then in fact. Glorification is not a metaphor. What the first covenant could not do, being weak through the flesh, God has done and will finish — and the confidence of the believer rests not on his progress but on the One who is able to keep.
roots_summary: Greek amemptos, unblamed — Hebrews 8:7; amomos, without blemish — Jude 24, Ephesians 5:27; Latin fallere, to fail, whence fault.
roots_lines: Greek amemptos — unblamed, giving no ground for censure; Hebrews 8:7 of the first covenant.
Greek amomos — without spot, the sacrificial term for an unblemished victim; Jude 24 and Ephesians 5:27.
Hebrew tamim — whole, entire, without blemish; the Levitical requirement for every offering.
Latin fallere, to fail or deceive, through Old French faute, a lack — the root of English fault.
Jude 24 assigns both verbs to God: He is able to keep and He shall present.
usage: “If that first covenant had been faultless” — the fault lay in the people, not the law.
“To present you faultless” — glorification stated as an act of God, not an attainment of man.
Amomos: the lamb without blemish, and the church presented in the same word.

pos: a. (liberal in giving; of the eye that looks on the poor and the man who will not be called so falsely)
etymology: From Old French bontif, kindly, from bonte, goodness, from Latin bonitas — with the English suffix -ful. The Hebrew at Proverbs 22:9 is literally tov ayin, a good eye; at Isaiah 32:5 the word is shoa, a man of substance or a noble.
biblical_def: Scripture locates generosity in the eye before it reaches the hand: “He that hath a bountiful eye shall be blessed; for he giveth of his bread to the poor” (Proverbs 22:9). The Hebrew is literally the good eye, standing over against the evil eye of the grudging man in Proverbs 23:6, and the idiom is exact — a man gives as he sees. The reason follows the promise: he is blessed for he giveth of his bread, so the blessing is not the motive but the consequence. Isaiah adds a warning about the word itself. In the day of the righteous king, “The vile person shall be no more called liberal, nor the churl said to be bountiful” (Isaiah 32:5) — that is, the flattering misuse of the word will end, and men will be named for what they are. Paul carries the whole doctrine into the collection for Jerusalem: “he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully” (2 Corinthians 9:6), and being “enriched in every thing to all bountifulness, which causeth through us thanksgiving to God” (2 Corinthians 9:11). The enriching is God's, the giving is the saint's, and the end of it is thanksgiving offered to God by those who received — not credit accruing to the giver.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bountiful as free to give, liberal in bestowing gifts and favors, and notes it is applied to the Creator as the giver of every good.
webster_full: BOUNTIFUL, a. Free to give; liberal in bestowing gifts and favors.
God, the bountiful author of our being.
2. Plentiful; abundant; as a bountiful supply of food.
BOUNTY, n. Liberality in bestowing gifts and favors; generosity; munificence.
Bounty differs from charity, as a genus from a species; charity being applied only to the relief of the poor.
scriptures: Proverbs 22:9
He that hath a bountiful eye shall be blessed; for he giveth of his bread to the poor.
Isaiah 32:5
The vile person shall be no more called liberal, nor the churl said to be bountiful.
2 Corinthians 9:6
But this I say, He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully.
2 Corinthians 9:11
Being enriched in every thing to all bountifulness, which causeth through us thanksgiving to God.
corruption_summary: 2 Corinthians 9:6 has been turned into a formula for personal enrichment, so that giving becomes an investment and God a debtor.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity teachers have made he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully into a transaction: money is sown into a ministry and a larger sum is expected back, with the promise underwritten by faith. The context destroys the reading. Paul is collecting for famine relief among poor saints in Jerusalem; the reaping he has in view he names two verses later — sufficiency in all things, that the giver may abound to every good work — and five verses later still the whole return is described as thanksgiving offered to God by the recipients. God enriches the giver in order to enlarge the giving, not to reward him for having given. A doctrine that makes the Almighty a debtor to His creature has abandoned grace at the root.

Isaiah 32:5 aims at a second corruption, and it is one every generation repeats: the flattery of the rich. The churl — the grasping man — was called bountiful because he had money and men wanted it, and the vile person was called liberal for the same reason. The promise of the righteous kingdom is that names will fit again. Proverbs locates the real thing in the eye, before any accounting: a good eye that sees the poor man, and a hand that parts with its own bread rather than its surplus.
roots_summary: Hebrew tov ayin, a good eye — Proverbs 22:9; shoa, a noble or man of substance — Isaiah 32:5; Greek haplotes, singleness or liberality — 2 Corinthians 9:11.
roots_lines: Hebrew tov ayin — literally “good of eye”; Proverbs 22:9, the idiom for a generous man.
Hebrew ra ayin — evil of eye, the grudging man; Proverbs 23:6, the exact opposite idiom.
Hebrew shoa — a man of substance, a noble; Isaiah 32:5, rendered bountiful.
Greek haplotes — singleness, simplicity, and so liberality; 2 Corinthians 9:11 and 8:2.
Greek eulogia — a blessing, and so a bounty; the word behind bountifully at 2 Corinthians 9:6.
usage: “A bountiful eye” — generosity begins in how a man sees before it reaches what he gives.
“Nor the churl said to be bountiful” — the end of flattering the grasping rich.
“Enriched in every thing to all bountifulness” — enriched in order to give, not in payment for giving.

pos: adv. (without mixture or pretence; of dealing done truly, and of preaching that is not)
etymology: From Latin sincerus, pure or unmixed — popularly, though doubtfully, derived from sine cera, without wax, the honey or marble unadulterated. The Greek is hagnos, pure, and eilikrineia, tested by sunlight and found unmixed.
biblical_def: The Authorized Version uses sincerely of dealing between men and of motive in preaching. Jotham presses the first upon the men of Shechem: “Now therefore, if ye have done truly and sincerely, in that ye have made Abimelech king, and if ye have dealt well with Jerubbaal and his house” (Judges 9:16). The whole parable of the trees hangs on that conditional, and the answer, as the chapter proves, is that they had not. The second is Paul's judgment on rival preachers at Philippi: “The one preach Christ of contention, not sincerely, supposing to add affliction to my bonds” (Philippians 1:16). It is a remarkable passage. Paul names their motive as bad, refuses to soften it, and then rejoices anyway that Christ is preached — holding both that the motive was corrupt and that the message was true. The related noun governs his own ministry: “we are not as many, which corrupt the word of God: but as of sincerity, but as of God, in the sight of God speak we in Christ” (2 Corinthians 2:17). The Greek eilikrineia pictures something held up to the sun and found without flaw or hidden filler. Sincerity in Scripture is therefore purity of substance, not warmth of feeling.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sincerely as honestly, with unfeigned reality, without hypocrisy or disguise.
webster_full: SINCERELY, adv. Honestly; with real purity of heart; without hypocrisy or disguise.
2. Unfeignedly; in reality.
SINCERE, a. Pure; unmixed. A joy sincere.
2. Being in reality what it appears to be; not feigned; not simulated.
3. Honest; artless; free from hypocrisy; as a sincere man.
scriptures: Judges 9:16

Now therefore, if ye have done truly and sincerely, in that ye have made Abimelech king, and if ye have dealt well with Jerubbaal and his house, and have done unto him according to the deserving of his hands;
Philippians 1:16
The one preach Christ of contention, not sincerely, supposing to add affliction to my bonds:
2 Corinthians 2:17
For we are not as many, which corrupt the word of God: but as of sincerity, but as of God, in the sight of God speak we in Christ.
1 Peter 2:2
As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby:
corruption_summary: Sincerity has been promoted from a quality of true doctrine to a substitute for it — as though meaning it earnestly made it so.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning error is that sincerity sanctifies belief: a man may hold anything provided he holds it honestly, and to question the content is to insult the person. This is not what the word means and it is not how Scripture uses it. Sincerus is unmixed; the question the word asks is about the substance, not the temperature. Paul in Philippians 1:16 is willing to say plainly that men preached Christ insincerely, from envy and contention, and he does not pretend otherwise to be gracious. Saul of Tarsus was entirely sincere on the Damascus road and entirely wrong, and it took the risen Christ to tell him so.

Peter supplies the corrective image: the sincere milk of the word — unadulterated, undiluted, nothing added for bulk. The old etymology of sine cera, without wax, may be false as a matter of Latin, but it is exactly right as a matter of doctrine: the corrupt merchant filled the cracks in inferior marble with wax and sold it as sound. Paul says that many corrupt the word of God after that manner, and sets over against it a ministry conducted in the sight of God. That is the test the word demands — not how strongly a thing is felt, but whether it is unmixed when held up to the light.
roots_summary: Greek eilikrineia, purity judged in sunlight — 2 Corinthians 2:17; adolos, unadulterated — 1 Peter 2:2; Latin sincerus, unmixed.
roots_lines: Greek eilikrineia — sincerity, from being tested by the light of the sun; 2 Corinthians 1:12 and 2:17.
Greek adolos — without guile or adulteration; 1 Peter 2:2, the sincere milk of the word.
Greek hagnos — pure, chaste; Philippians 1:17 of preaching done in love.
Hebrew tamim — whole, entire; Judges 9:16, rendered sincerely alongside truly.
Latin sincerus — unmixed, pure; the popular gloss sine cera, without wax, is doubtful Latin but sound doctrine.
usage: “If ye have done truly and sincerely” — Jotham's conditional, which Shechem failed.
“The one preach Christ of contention, not sincerely” — Paul names the motive and rejoices in the message.
“The sincere milk of the word” — unmixed, with nothing added for bulk.

pos: adv. (with heat; of prayer laboured over and of love stretched to its full strength)
etymology: From Latin fervere, to boil or glow, through fervens, boiling. The Greek at Colossians 4:12 is agonizomai, to contend as in the games; at 1 Peter 1:22 it is ektenos, stretched out to the utmost.
biblical_def: The word names heat, and Scripture applies it to two things chiefly — prayer and love. Epaphras is commended for the first: “always labouring fervently for you in prayers, that ye may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God” (Colossians 4:12). The Greek verb is agonizomai, the word for a wrestler in the arena; Epaphras is not described as feeling deeply but as contending, and the object of his contest is the maturity of a church he is not present with. Peter applies it to love: “see that ye love one another with a pure heart fervently” (1 Peter 1:22), where ektenos means stretched out at full extension, like a runner at the tape or a muscle at its limit. Both words are athletic, and both are commanded, which tells against any notion that fervency is a temperament some men are born with and others are not. James adds the promise: “The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much” (James 5:16). Apollos is described in the same register as “fervent in the spirit” (Acts 18:25) even before his instruction was complete. Heat without doctrine is dangerous; doctrine without heat is dead; the New Testament requires both.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fervently as with great heat, and figuratively with earnestness, ardor, and warm zeal.
webster_full: FERVENTLY, adv. With great heat.
2. With earnestness; eagerly; vehemently; with great warmth.
Epaphras, a servant of Christ, saluteth you, always laboring fervently for you in prayers.
FERVENT, a. Hot; boiling; as fervent heat.
2. Warm in feeling; ardent in temperament; earnest; excited; animated; glowing; as fervent zeal.
scriptures: Colossians 4:12
Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ, saluteth you, always labouring fervently for you in prayers, that ye may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God.
1 Peter 1:22
Seeing ye have purified your souls in obeying the truth through the Spirit unto unfeigned love of the brethren, see that ye love one another with a pure heart fervently:
James 5:16
Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.
Acts 18:25
This man was instructed in the way of the Lord; and being fervent in the spirit, he spake and taught diligently the things of the Lord, knowing only the baptism of John.
corruption_summary: Fervency has been reduced to an emotional pitch produced in a meeting, rather than the sustained labour Scripture actually names.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern usage measures fervency by volume and visible feeling, and the machinery of contemporary worship is built to manufacture it — lighting, dynamics, and repetition arranged to produce a state the participants then take for the presence of God. The words the apostles use point somewhere else entirely. Agonizomai is the wrestler's word; ektenos is the word for a limb stretched to its limit. Both describe effort sustained over time, most of it unwitnessed. Epaphras's fervency was exercised for a congregation he was away from, in prayers nobody heard, over a period long enough for Paul to call it always.

The corrective is not coldness. Reformed men, reacting against manufactured emotion, sometimes settle for a religion of correct propositions held without heat, and Scripture rebukes that as sharply as it rebukes the other error — the Laodicean is spued out for being lukewarm, not for being unsound. James is blunt about what fervent prayer accomplishes: it availeth much. Fervency in the biblical sense is measured by what a man will keep doing when no one is watching and nothing is felt, which is a far more searching test than any meeting can apply.
roots_summary: Greek agonizomai, to contend as in the games — Colossians 4:12; ektenos, stretched out at full extent — 1 Peter 1:22; zeo, to boil — Acts 18:25.
roots_lines: Greek agonizomai — to struggle, to contend for a prize; Colossians 4:12 of Epaphras at prayer.
Greek ektenos — stretched out to the utmost; 1 Peter 1:22 and 4:8, of love at full extension.
Greek energeo — to be operative, to work effectually; the participle behind effectual fervent at James 5:16.
Greek zeo — to boil, to be hot; Acts 18:25 of Apollos, and Romans 12:11, “fervent in spirit.”
Latin fervere, to boil — the source of the English word and of fervour.
usage: “Labouring fervently for you in prayers” — the wrestler's word, applied to intercession.
“Love one another with a pure heart fervently” — love stretched to its full extension.
“The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much” — heat with a promise attached.
